metadata.description: Active-negative pair: paper A is a tutorial on spectral clustering (graph Laplacians, RatioCut/Ncut relaxation, spectral embedding + k-means), paper B is the Candes-Tao decoding-by-linear-programming paper that founds compressed sensing (RIP/ROP, basis pursuit, LP decoder, exact sparse recovery). Both rely on linear algebra and (in B) sparsity, but the mathematical objects (graph Laplacian eigenvectors and trace-relaxed cuts vs restricted-isometry constants and l1 dual certificates), the problems (unsupervised partitioning vs sparse recovery from corrupted linear measurements) and the proof techniques (block-diagonal spectra and Rayleigh-Ritz vs iterative dual-certificate construction and Gaussian concentration) have no node-level correspondence. All paper-origin Level-1 nodes on both sides are unmatched.

matches.explanation: Similarity graph $G=(V,E)$ built from data points with weighted edges. Paper B has no graph-theoretic data structure; its primitives are the coding matrix $A$ and the annihilator/measurement matrix $F$, which are not pairwise-similarity graphs.
Weighted adjacency matrix $W$ of an undirected graph. No counterpart in paper B: $A$ is a coding/measurement matrix indexing $\R^n \to \R^m$, not a vertex-by-vertex symmetric similarity matrix.

Vertex degree and diagonal degree matrix $D$. Paper B has no notion of vertex degree; the only diagonal-matrix-like objects are subset-restricted Gramians $F_T^* F_T$, which are spectra-of-submatrices, not row-sum normalisers.

Indicator vector $\charfct_A$ and volume $\vol(A)=\sum_{i\in A} d_i$ of a vertex subset. Paper B uses indicator-style constructions only via supports of sparse vectors (sets $T \subset J$), which are unrelated to vertex-volume measures.
Connected components and partitions of the vertex set. Paper B has no graph-theoretic notion of connectivity; subsets there are sparsity supports, not topologically connected pieces.
$\epsilon$-neighborhood graph construction. Paper B has no neighbor/distance-thresholding graph construction at all.
$k$-NN graph construction. No counterpart in paper B.
Mutual $k$-NN graph construction. No counterpart in paper B.

Fully connected graph with Gaussian similarity. Paper B's only random-matrix construction is i.i.d. Gaussian entries of $F$ (Theorem 1.5 / Lemma 3.1) — a measurement matrix, not a pairwise-similarity graph.

Unnormalized graph Laplacian $\Lun = D-W$. The central object of paper A. Paper B has no Laplacian-type operator; its analogous central object is the restricted-isometry-constant collection $\delta_S, \theta_{S,S'}$ on submatrices of $F$, which has a completely different role (controlling sparse-vector geometry, not encoding combinatorial connectivity).
Symmetric and random-walk normalized Laplacians $\Lsym, \Lrw$. No counterpart in paper B.
Cut value $\Cut(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$. Paper B has no graph-cut objective; its objectives are $\ell_0$ / $\ell_1$ norms of sparse vectors.
Random-walk transition matrix $P=D^{-1}W$ and its stationary distribution $\pi_i = d_i/\vol(V)$. No Markov-chain object appears in paper B.

Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse $\Lun^\dagger$ of the unnormalized Laplacian. Paper B does invert $F_T^* F_T$ inside the dual-certificate construction (Lemma 2.1), but that is a full inverse on a sparsity-restricted submatrix, not a spectral pseudo-inverse of a Laplacian.

Properties of $\Lun$: quadratic-form expansion, symmetry, PSD, smallest eigenvalue 0 with constant eigenvector. Paper B has no analogous structural-properties statement; its lemmas (LP2.1-LP2.5) all concern restricted-isometry/orthogonality bounds, not spectral structure of a fixed Laplacian.

Multiplicity-of-zero theorem: dim ker $\Lun$ = number of connected components, eigenspace spanned by component indicators. The defining structural fact of spectral clustering. No counterpart in paper B; its closest 'kernel' statement (LP2.2: $\delta_{2S}<1$ implies unique sparse representations) concerns injectivity of submatrices of $F$ on sparse vectors, not combinatorial connectivity.
Properties of normalized Laplacians: quadratic form, $\Lsym$-$\Lrw$ eigen-correspondence, PSD. No counterpart in paper B.
Multiplicity-of-zero theorem for normalized Laplacians. No counterpart in paper B.

Mincut problem: partition vertex set to minimise total cut weight. Paper B's problems (ProbP2.1 linear-code decoding, ProbP2.2 $\ell_0$-min, ProbP2.3 basis pursuit, ProbP2.4 direct LP decoding) all concern recovery of vectors from linear measurements — entirely different decision variables (sparse error vector vs vertex partition).
RatioCut minimisation, equivalently $\min_H \Tr(H'\Lun H)$ s.t. $H'H=I$. NP-hard combinatorial. No counterpart in paper B.
Ncut minimisation. No counterpart in paper B.

Spectral relaxation of RatioCut: $\min \Tr(H'\Lun H)$ s.t. $H'H=I$, solved by bottom-$k$ eigenvectors. Both papers feature 'relaxations' — paper B's $\ell_0\to\ell_1$ basis-pursuit relaxation (ProbP2.3) is also a tractable relaxation of an NP-hard combinatorial problem — but the structural mathematics differs (continuous trace minimisation solved by eigenvalues, vs LP relaxation solved by simplex/interior-point), and the relaxation guarantees are very different (no general approximation factor for spectral, exact under RIP for $\ell_1$). The conceptual analogy is too superficial to justify even an `analogous` match.
Spectral relaxation of Ncut as a generalized eigenproblem $\Lun u = \lambda Du$. No counterpart in paper B.

Unnormalized spectral clustering algorithm: build similarity graph, eigendecompose $\Lun$, embed, $k$-means. Paper B's algorithm (AP2.1) is the LP decoder that solves $\min \|y-Ag\|_{\ell_1}$. No shared computational primitive: eigendecomposition + Lloyd vs simplex/interior-point on a linear program.
Proof of properties of $\Lun$ via direct expansion of $f'\Lun f = f'Df - f'Wf$. Paper B has no proofs of Laplacian-quadratic-form identities.
Proof of components-vs-spectrum via block-diagonal structure of $\Lun$. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of properties of $\Lsym, \Lrw$ via algebraic eigenvalue manipulations. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of components-vs-spectrum for normalized Laplacians. No counterpart in paper B.
Proof of $\Ncut = P(\bar A|A)+P(A|\bar A)$ via stationary-distribution computation. No counterpart in paper B.
Quadratic form $f'\Lun f = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j} w_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2$. No counterpart in paper B.
RatioCut indicator vector encoding for $k=2$. No counterpart in paper B.
Reformulation $f'\Lun f = |V|\cdot\Ratiocut(A,\bar A)$. No counterpart in paper B.
Volume-weighted indicator vector for binary Ncut. No counterpart in paper B.

Open problem: theory of similarity-graph choice (graph type, $k, \eps, \sigma$) for spectral clustering. Paper B's open problem (OpenP2.1, tight cut-off and finite-alphabet decoding) is on a completely different axis.
Open problem: tight relation between spectral clustering and commute distance. No counterpart in paper B.
Open problem: interaction between number of clusters $k$ and graph connectivity parameters. No counterpart in paper B.
Linear-code decoding problem: recover $f$ from $y=Af+e$ with sparse $e$. Paper A has no error-correction or sparse-recovery problem; its problems are graph-partitioning.

$\ell_0$-minimization $(P_0)$: NP-hard combinatorial sparsest-solution problem. Paper A's NP-hard combinatorial problems (ProbP1.2/ProbP1.3) are graph cuts; the optimization variable is a vertex partition rather than a sparse vector. Different category of combinatorial problem.
Basis Pursuit $(P_1)$: $\ell_1$-relaxation of $(P_0)$ as a linear program. No counterpart in paper A.
Direct decoding LP $(P'_1)$: $\min \|y-Ag\|_{\ell_1}$. No counterpart in paper A.

Restricted Isometry Constants $\delta_S$. The cornerstone definition of paper B (and of compressed sensing as a field). No counterpart in paper A; spectral clustering uses full-spectrum eigenvalues of a fixed Laplacian, not subset-uniform isometry bounds on submatrices.
Restricted Orthogonality Constants $\theta_{S,S'}$. No counterpart in paper A.
Compressible-signal class $\cF_s(B)$ with power-law sorted-magnitude decay. No counterpart in paper A.
Sparsity assumption $\|e\|_{\ell_0} \le \rho m$. No counterpart in paper A.
Annihilator reduction $FA=0 \Rightarrow Fy=Fe$. No counterpart in paper A.
LP form of $(P'_1)$ with slack variable $t$ and constraint $-t \le y-Ag \le t$. No counterpart in paper A.
Unit-norm characterisation of $\delta_1$. No counterpart in paper A.
Sufficient condition $\delta_S+\delta_{2S}+\delta_{3S} < \rho_{p/m}(r)$ under the Gaussian model. No counterpart in paper A.
Theta-delta comparison $\theta_{S,S'} \le \delta_{S+S'} \le \theta_{S,S'}+\max(\delta_S,\delta_{S'})$. No counterpart in paper A.
Unique sparse-recovery lemma: $\delta_{2S}<1 \Rightarrow$ unique sparse representations. No counterpart in paper A.
Dual sparse reconstruction property, $\ell_2$ version (Lemma 2.1). No counterpart in paper A; spectral clustering does not employ dual-certificate constructions.
Dual sparse reconstruction property, $\ell_\infty$ version (Lemma 2.2). No counterpart in paper A.

Uniform Gaussian RIP bound (Lemma 3.1) via union-bound + entropy + Ledoux concentration. Paper A discusses Gaussian random matrices only as similarity-graph weights (DP1.9), with no concentration analysis on submatrix spectra.

Main recovery theorem: $\delta_S+\theta_S+\theta_{S,2S}<1 \Rightarrow$ $\ell_1$-min exactly recovers any $S$-sparse vector. The headline theorem of paper B. Paper A has no exact-recovery theorem of this type; its strongest result (PrP1.2) is the connected-components / kernel characterization, which is structural rather than recovery-theoretic.
Decoding theorem (Theorem 1.4): under the RIP+ROP condition, $(P'_1)$ exactly recovers $f$ despite arbitrary $S$-sparse corruption. No counterpart in paper A.
Gaussian matrices satisfy main hypothesis (Theorem 1.5) with overwhelming probability for $r < r^*(p,m)$. No counterpart in paper A.
Optimal recovery of compressible signals: $\sup \|\alpha-\alpha^\sharp\| \le C(K/\lambda)^{-(s-1/2)}$ over the power-law class. No counterpart in paper A.
Gaussian decoding corollary: for Gaussian $A$ with $p=m-n$, $(P'_1)$ recovers $f$ exactly under the hypotheses of Theorem 1.5. No counterpart in paper A.

LP decoder for $(P'_1)$: solve $\min 1^T t$ s.t. $-t \le y-Ag \le t$. Paper A's algorithms (AP1.1) are eigendecompose + $k$-means; no shared computational machinery (LP simplex/interior-point vs eigensolver+Lloyd).
Proof of unique-sparse-recovery lemma (LP2.2) by contradiction using $\delta_{2S}<1$. No counterpart in paper A.
Proof of Lemma 2.1: explicit construction $w := F_T(F_T^*F_T)^{-1} c_T$ as a dual certificate, with duality bounds. No counterpart in paper A.

Proof of Lemma 2.2 by iterative correction $w := \sum_n (-1)^{n-1} w_n$ with geometric-series control. No counterpart in paper A; spectral clustering proofs are algebraic (block-diagonal expansions) rather than iterative.
Proof of Theorem 1.3 via dual-certificate $\ell_1$ comparison forcing $d=c$. No counterpart in paper A.
Proof of theta-delta comparison via parallelogram identity. No counterpart in paper A.
Proof of Lemma 3.1: union bound over $\binom{m}{S}$ subsets + Stirling entropy estimate + Ledoux concentration. No counterpart in paper A.
Open problem: tight cut-off threshold and finite-alphabet extensions of LP decoding. No counterpart in paper A.
